what-is-the-science-of-learning:
The findings that hold up across settings, and how they apply to a child rather than to a student in a laboratory. Four of them are unusually well replicated.

Spacing

The same total study time produces more durable learning when spread out than when massed together. This is one of the most replicated findings in psychology.

At home: five minutes on something most days beats forty minutes on Sunday. Revisit last week's material briefly rather than only the new thing.

The counterintuitive part is that spacing feels worse while you do it. Massed practice produces a comfortable sense of fluency that does not survive a week.

Retrieval

Being made to recall something strengthens it more than reading it again. Testing is not only measurement; it is one of the better ways to learn.

At home: close the book and ask them to tell you. Ask what they remember from yesterday. "Explain it to me without looking" is retrieval practice and a comprehension check at once.

This also has the reverse implication: re-reading notes, the most common revision method, is among the least effective.

Elaboration

Asking why and how, connecting new material to what is already known, improves retention. Isolated facts are hard to hold; connected ones are not.

At home: why do you think that happens. What does that remind you of. How does that fit with the other thing you told me.

Worked examples

For a beginner, studying a fully worked example is more effective than attempting a problem unaided. Once some competence exists, the balance reverses and problem-solving becomes more useful.

At home: show the whole thing first with a novice, rather than setting them off to discover it. Then withdraw as they gain ground.

This is one place where research disagrees with a common instinct about discovery learning, and the resolution is that it depends on prior knowledge.

Two others worth knowing

Interleaving: mixing problem types rather than doing twenty of the same. Harder, feels worse, produces better transfer.

Desirable difficulty: the general principle behind all of the above. Conditions that make learning feel harder often make it stick better, and conditions that feel fluent often do not.

The important caveat

Most of this comes from laboratory studies, often with older students and simple material. Effects in real classrooms are usually smaller and less reliable.

And none of it substitutes for knowledge. These are techniques for learning things; they do not tell you what is worth learning, and a child with excellent technique and no background knowledge is not well placed.

The single most useful takeaway for a family: ask them to tell you without looking, regularly. It is retrieval, spacing and elaboration in one question.
what-does-neuroscience-say-about-child-d:
What brain science genuinely establishes about childhood, and the considerable gap between that and the claims made in its name. This is a field where the popular version has run a long way ahead of the research.

What is reasonably established

The brain develops for a long time. Structural maturation continues into the mid-twenties, with the prefrontal regions associated with planning and impulse control among the last. This is real and it is the single most useful fact for a parent.

Experience shapes structure. Synaptic connections are formed and pruned in response to use. What a child does affects how their brain develops.

Some periods are more sensitive than others. Vision and language have windows during which typical input matters particularly. This is well supported for these specific systems.

Severe deprivation causes lasting harm. The research on children raised in profoundly neglectful institutions is unambiguous and it is one of the strongest findings in the field.

Sleep matters for consolidation. Memory consolidation during sleep is well evidenced.

What is claimed and is not established

The first three years determine everything. An overstatement of the sensitive period research. The brain remains plastic and change remains possible. This claim has caused genuine anxiety in parents for no good reason.

Left-brained and right-brained people. Not a thing. Functions are lateralised to a degree; people are not.

Learning styles. Visual, auditory and kinaesthetic learners. Repeatedly tested, repeatedly unsupported, still taught.

We use ten per cent of our brains. No.

Specific products build specific brain areas. Almost never demonstrated, frequently asserted.

Brain scans show a child is behind. Group averages do not diagnose individuals, and the imaging cannot do what the marketing implies.

The structural problem

Neuroscience carries authority, so attaching it to a claim makes the claim sound better established than it is. Studies have found that adding irrelevant neuroscience to an explanation makes people rate it more convincing.

That is exactly why the field attracts overstatement, and why a parent should be more sceptical when brain imaging is mentioned rather than less.

How to read a headline

Ask: was this in humans or animals. How many participants. Does it show correlation or intervention. Does the finding actually support the practical advice attached to it, or is the advice a leap.

Most of the gap between research and headline occurs in that last step.

What actually follows for a parent

Very little that is surprising, which is itself informative. Relationships, sleep, conversation, play, and not being frightened by claims about windows closing.

The genuine neuroscience mostly supports what developmental psychology already said. When it appears to support something startling, that is usually the reporting rather than the research.
how-does-movement-help-children-learn:
The links between physical activity, attention and memory, stated at the strength the evidence supports, which is more modest than the popular version and still worth acting on.

Reasonably well supported

Acute effects on attention. A bout of moderate physical activity is associated with better attention and executive function in the period immediately afterwards. Effects are short-lived and reasonably consistent across studies.

The practical implication is specific: movement before a demanding task, not as a reward after it.

Sleep. Physically active children fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply, and sleep affects attention, mood and memory consolidation. This chain is the most reliable route from movement to learning.

The foundation for handwriting. Climbing, hanging and carrying build trunk and shoulder stability. A child without it cannot sit comfortably or steady a hand, and this is a genuine and under-recognised cause of writing difficulty.

Mood. Consistent associations between activity and lower rates of anxiety and low mood in children.

Where the evidence is thinner

That exercise raises academic attainment. The association exists and is modest. Intervention studies adding physical activity to school days show inconsistent effects on attainment, partly because the time comes from somewhere.

That specific movement programmes improve reading. Various commercial programmes claim this. Evidence is weak.

Brain gym and similar exercises. Not supported.

That crawling is necessary for later reading. A persistent claim with no good evidence behind it.

The embodied cognition point

There is real research suggesting that gesture and physical action support learning of certain concepts, particularly spatial and mathematical ones. Children who gesture while explaining tend to understand better, and encouraging gesture can help.

This is genuine and it is narrower than the sweeping claims sometimes built on it.

What follows practically

Movement before homework rather than after. Outdoor time daily, which does several of these jobs at once. Climbing and hanging specifically, for the postural foundation. Breaks in long tasks. And not treating physical activity as the thing to cut when academic pressure rises, which is the standard response and is counterproductive.

The honest summary

Movement is not a learning intervention with a large effect on attainment. It is a precondition for a child being in a state where learning is possible, and it improves sleep, mood, attention and the physical foundation for writing.

That is a strong enough case without overstating it.
does-starting-school-earlier-help-childr:
Countries start formal schooling anywhere between four and seven. What the comparative evidence shows about long-run outcomes, and what it genuinely cannot settle.

The starting positions

England and parts of Australia begin formal instruction at four or five. Much of Scandinavia and Eastern Europe begins at six or seven, with the preceding years in kindergarten focused on play, language and social development.

This is a natural experiment, which is why it attracts attention, and it is a badly controlled one, which is why it settles less than people claim.

What the evidence suggests

Early starters are ahead early. Unsurprisingly. A child taught to read at five reads earlier than one taught at seven.

The gap tends to close. Studies following children to around age eleven generally find the early advantage diminished or gone. Finland, starting at seven, reaches high literacy by adolescence.

Some evidence on attitudes. Research comparing children who began formal reading at five with those who began at seven found similar reading ability by around eleven, and less positive attitudes to reading in the early group. Finding this deserves caution: it is one line of work, not a consensus.

Relative age effects are robust. Within any school year, the youngest children are consistently more likely to be identified as struggling or as having special needs. This effect is well replicated across countries and fades over years without disappearing quickly.

What the comparison cannot settle

This is the important part.

Countries differ in nearly everything: teacher training and status, class size, child poverty, parental leave, healthcare, language transparency. Finnish orthography is far more regular than English, which alone affects how long learning to read takes.

Attributing outcome differences to starting age specifically is not something these comparisons can do.

What can reasonably be said

Starting later does not appear to cause lasting harm. Starting earlier does not appear to confer lasting advantage. The quality of what happens matters more than the age at which it starts.

And within a system, the younger children in a year group face a real and measurable disadvantage that is frequently mistaken for a difficulty in the child.

What follows for a parent

Almost nothing about the school system, which you do not control.

What is useful: if your child is among the youngest in their year and is finding the first years hard, that is very often relative age rather than a problem with them, and it evens out.

And the years before formal school are not preparation to be filled with early academics. Language, play, sound awareness and attention are what the later reading is built on.
